name: Sara Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential and won’t be linked to your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the orthopaedic ward at Brookfield County Hospital, which is in the town I grew up in. Mostly it's older people with broken hips, plus knee and hip replacements, the odd young lad off a motorbike. A normal day is pain relief, checking circulation in legs and feet, getting people up with the physios, and a lot of lifting and turning, even with the hoists. I do long days, three or four a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing someone go home on their own two feet after they came in on a trolley crying. I'm not a computer person and I still write my own handover on a folded sheet of paper. What wears me out is the lifting, my back's already complaining at 27, and money. My partner Liam's an apprentice electrician, so his pay's low for another year, and we've basically got nothing put by. My mum's ten minutes away, which is the main reason I'd never leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it out as it's written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. Fine by me, honestly. I'd quite like things to stay as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and I'd say it quietly, because I don't really do arguments about this stuff. If someone at work brought it up I'd shrug and say the hips still need fixing. I don't post things online, I just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like my job the way it is. If AI turns out to be hype, I'll be the least surprised person on the orthopaedic ward. The only thing is, staying the same means staying skint until Liam qualifies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd carry on with my long days and keep my paper handover. Liam and I would keep doing what we do, which is one big shop a week and no holidays this year, and wait for his pay rise when he finishes his apprenticeship next autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved. A bit bored by the whole question, if I'm being honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one bad month look like for the two of you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Liam's van broke down or the landlord put the rent up again. We'd ask my mum, which I hate. Or I'd do an extra long day a week, which my back wouldn't thank me for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine bit of your job you'd be happy to see a computer take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The falls risk forms, maybe. We fill in the same one three times a day and nobody reads it. If AI can do that, it can have it.

say: I'd say I'm **not surprised**, but quietly, because I avoid arguments about it.
I'd tell colleagues the **broken hips** still need fixing whatever happens.
think: I **like my job** as it is and would welcome nothing changing.
Staying the same also means staying **skint** until my partner qualifies.
do: Carry on with **long days** and the paper handover sheet.
Stick to **one big shop** a week and no holiday this year.
Wait for her partner's **pay rise** when his apprenticeship ends next autumn.
feel: **Relieved** that her ward stays as it is.
A bit **bored** by the whole AI question.
S0.quote: I like my job the way it is. If AI turns out to be hype, I'll be the least surprised person on the orthopaedic ward.
fieldNote: Her job feels safe; unease comes from **thin money** and her partner's apprentice wage.
She's **quiet** about her views and reads rather than posts online.
Her back at 27 is a **hidden worry** she mentions almost in passing.

steps.text: Carry on with long days and the paper handover sheet
Keep to one weekly shop and skip a holiday this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That sounds more likely than the first one, I'll give you that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nursing will be fine because it's hands-on, and that's what I'd tell my mum when she asked. At work I'd probably go along with whatever new system they brought in, without complaining much. I'm not the one who makes a fuss in meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd dread the training. I write my handover on a folded sheet of paper in my pocket, and I'd keep doing that until somebody took the pen off me. I'm not worried about losing my job, I'm worried about looking slow in front of the students.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training when it's compulsory and not before. I'd ask Priti, the ward sister, to show me the new system on a quiet shift, because I won't ask in front of everyone. Money-wise nothing changes, so I'd just keep waiting on Liam's pay rise and see how it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit embarrassed in advance. Calm about my job, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else on the ward comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our ward clerk, Sandra, who books all the follow-up clinics. That's exactly the sort of booking job the card says goes first. She's been there 20 years and she'd be lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd see how it goes. How would you know it was time to do something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they stopped replacing nurses who leave. That's what I'd watch. Two people gone and nobody new, that's when I'd start looking at the job adverts properly.

say: I'd say nursing will be fine because it's **hands-on** work.
I'd go along with **new systems** at work without making a fuss.
think: I'd **dread the training** and keep my paper handover as long as I could.
My fear is **looking slow** in front of students, not losing my job.
do: Do the **compulsory training** only when it's required.
Ask the **ward sister** privately to show her the system on a quiet shift.
Watch whether leavers stop being **replaced** before doing anything else.
feel: A bit **embarrassed** in advance about learning in public.
S1.quote: I write my handover on a folded sheet of paper in my pocket, and I'd keep doing that until somebody took the pen off me.
fieldNote: Her worry is **pride** and looking slow, not losing work; she feels her job is hands-on.
She sets a clear **trigger**: two leavers not replaced means it's time to look.
She thinks of the **ward clerk** first, someone whose booking work is exposed.

steps.text: Keep working long days on the orthopaedic ward
Watch whether nurses who leave get replaced before acting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's quick. And robots three years after that, 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening and that the government should slow it down, but I wouldn't march about it. I'd tell my mum not to worry. At work I'd say "we'll see", because that's what I say about everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork side goes in 2028, which doesn't bother me, I hate it anyway. What bothers me is 2031, when they've got robots that can lift and turn a hip patient. Lifting and turning is half my day. Two years isn't long enough for me to become a different kind of person, so I'd nurse, save every penny, and hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop buying anything that isn't food or rent, starting that week. I'd try to save 100 a month, which I've never managed. Liam and I would talk about moving in with my mum for a year to build something up. And I'd keep doing my job and wait to see what the hospital actually decides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A tight feeling in my chest, like before a ward inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean for your work that the thinking AI arrives three years before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means for three years I'd be doing only the heavy bits. No forms, no computer, just washing, lifting and walking people. My back's bad already, so honestly I'm not sure I'd last the three years either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with your mum. How would Liam feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd go along with it, but he wouldn't like it. Mum talks a lot and he's a quiet one. We'd give it a year and see, and I'd tell him it's that or no savings at all.

say: I'd say it's **frightening** and government should slow it down, without marching about it.
I'd tell colleagues **"we'll see"**, as she says about everything.
think: Robots by **2031** could do the lifting and turning that fills half her day.
Two years is too short to **become different**, so she'd nurse, save and hope.
do: Stop buying anything **beyond food and rent** from that week.
Try to save **100 a month** for the first time.
Consider **moving in** with her mum for a year to build savings.
feel: **Anxious**, with a tight chest like before a ward inspection.
S2.quote: Two years isn't long enough for me to become a different kind of person, so I'd nurse, save every penny, and hope.
fieldNote: She's not afraid of the **paperwork** going; the robots that lift worry her.
Her **bad back** makes even the three-year gap feel uncertain.
Her plan is mostly **saving and waiting**, true to her resistance to change.

steps.text: Stop all spending beyond food and rent from that week
Save 100 a month for the first time
Move in with her mum for a year with her partner
Wait to see what Brookfield hospital decides about staffing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. 2031, and robots by 2034. That's a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that it's worrying but there's time, and the hospitals and government should be sorting out a plan. I'd go to an information session if they held one. I'd sit at the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum always said save for a rainy day, and I've never had anything to save. Five years would make me start. Liam would be qualified by then and doing proper electrician's work, which robots will take a while to do in old houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once Liam's pay goes up next autumn, I'd put his rise straight into savings and pretend we never had it. I'd look into the fracture clinic at the hospital, the outpatient side, because it's lighter on my back. I'd probably not do any AI courses unless they made me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less than with two years. I can breathe a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the fracture clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's nine to five, no lifting, and it's mostly talking to people and checking plaster. I've always thought about it for my back. AI coming would just be the push I'd need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do AI courses unless they made you. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm truthful. I'd do what's needed for the job. I'm not going to become the expert, that's for the younger ones who enjoy it.

say: I'd say it's worrying but there's **time**, and hospitals should plan now.
I'd go to an **information session**, sitting at the back.
think: Five years would finally make me **start saving**, as my mum always said.
Her partner would be **qualified** by then, in work robots won't reach quickly.
do: Put her partner's **pay rise** straight into savings next autumn.
Look into a move to the **fracture clinic**, which is lighter on her back.
Avoid **AI courses** unless the hospital makes them compulsory.
feel: **Worried**, but able to breathe more than with two years.
S3.quote: My mum always said save for a rainy day, and I've never had anything to save. Five years would make me start.
fieldNote: Her partner's **qualification** is the household's real safety plan.
The **fracture clinic** idea is about her back, with AI only the push.
She stays **resistant** to AI courses even with five years, and says so plainly.

steps.text: Save her partner's apprenticeship pay rise from next autumn
Ask about a move to the hospital's fracture clinic

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. 2036, robots 2039. I'd be 37. That sounds far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, the hospital will sort it out. I'd probably sound more relaxed than I am. That's how I am about most things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough for me to talk myself out of doing anything. I know that about myself. I'd keep saying next year, and suddenly it would be 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am on the ward. I'd keep putting Liam's pay rise aside once it comes. Maybe in a few years I'd look at the fracture clinic. Otherwise I'd wait and see what the hospital does, which I know isn't much of a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A small nagging feeling, like a bill on the side you haven't opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would give you the push you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Liam, probably. Or Priti, the ward sister, who's always on at me to do more courses. My mum would just tell me not to worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would make you feel properly secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Having three months' money in the bank. That's it, really. If I had that, I wouldn't care much whether it was ten years or twenty.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** and the hospital will sort it out.
I'd sound more **relaxed** than I really feel.
think: Ten years lets me **talk myself out** of doing anything.
I'd keep saying **next year** until it was 2035.
do: Carry on working on the **orthopaedic ward** as now.
Save her partner's **pay rise** once it comes through.
Maybe look at the **fracture clinic** in a few years' time.
feel: Mostly **okay**, with a small nagging feeling like an unopened bill.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough for me to talk myself out of doing anything. I know that about myself.
fieldNote: She knows her own habit of **putting things off** and names it.
**Three months' savings** is her own definition of feeling secure.
Her job feels safe for now; her unease is the **thin cushion**, not AI.

steps.text: Carry on working on the orthopaedic ward as now
Put her partner's pay rise into savings once it arrives
Wait to see the hospital's plans before acting

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of the robots in 2031 doing the lifting, and my back, and no money behind us. What would help is having three months in the bank, and the hospital moving people like me into clinics or lighter jobs instead of just letting us go. Robots can lift a hip patient, maybe. Nobody's built a robot yet that a scared 90-year-old woman will let hold her hand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Probably about my back. Nobody asks nurses about their bodies. Half of us will be worn out before any robot gets here.

headlineQuote: Robots can lift a hip patient, maybe. Nobody's built a robot yet that a scared 90-year-old woman will let hold her hand.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old orthopaedic nurse** in her hometown hospital, ten minutes from her mum.
She's **not a computer person** and still writes her handover on folded paper.
Her partner Liam is an **apprentice electrician**, and they have almost nothing saved.
She stays uneasy in mild pictures and **anxious** under fast AGI, mostly saving and waiting.
Her **bad back** worries her as much as any robot.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots doing the lifting by 2031 would hit half her day with no savings behind her.
whatWouldHelp: The hospital moving nurses into **clinics or lighter jobs** instead of letting them go.
